clue.text: Elephantine character portrayed in hospital by playwright

parts.note: H is the standard abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

explanation.walkthrough: 'in' joins the pieces: H then ORTON, side by side. The answer is the elephant of Dr Seuss's Horton Hears a Who!, the puzzle's theme author.
explanation.definitionFit: Horton is the kindly elephant hero of two Dr Seuss picture books.

clue.text: Symbols of a war arising in part from intense sorrow

explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'arising' means reading upwards, so SESOR, inside 'intense sorrow', reads backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The Wars of the Roses took their name from the white and red flower badges of York and Lancaster.

taken as written

clue.text: Migrants going wrong about second language thus?

explanation.definitionFit: Theodor Geisel wrote his rhyming children's books in verse under this pen name, so he is a poet.

clue.text: Number to get angry we hear about attribute of Father Brown

explanation.definitionFit: Chesterton's priest sleuth is defined by an unworldly guilelessness in the title of his first book.

clue.text: Eccentric timeless elegist? Humorist rather

parts.note: taken as written
time is abbreviated t, and timeless says that letter must come out

explanation.surface: An odd poet of laments with no sense of time is really more a comic writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Take T out of ELEGIST and rearrange the remaining ELEGIS. Theodor Geisel was the real name of Dr Seuss.
explanation.definitionFit: Theodor Geisel wrote comic verse and cartoons, so he was a writer of comedy.

clue.text: Comic character of article about colour with zeal to capture hearts

explanation.definitionFit: The mischievous striped-hat feline of Dr Seuss's 1957 book is a comical figure.

clue.text: With which to illuminate Bergman movie at start of scene

explanation.surface: Lighting a film set for an Ingrid Bergman picture, right from the opening scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Victorian streets and rooms were lit by gas lamps, so these are things used for lighting.

clue.text: Whence one is returning with injunctions initially ten in number

definitions.text: Whence one is returning with injunctions initially ten in number

parts.note: an is the indefinite article, meaning one
taken as written

indicators.note: initially picks only the opening letter of the word injunctions

explanation.surface: Moses comes back down the mountain carrying the Ten Commandments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' turns AN IS into SINA; add the first letter of 'injunctions'. The whole clue also describes the place: Moses came down from it with tablets of ten commandments.
explanation.definitionFit: Mount Sinai is where, in Exodus, Moses received the Ten Commandments before coming down.

clue.text: Part taken by Michell as King, e.g. Harold

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An actor named Michell plays a king, a role such as Harold.
explanation.walkthrough: Keith Michell famously played Henry VIII, so 'e.g. Harold' reads as another king; it is in fact the political theorist Harold Laski.
explanation.definitionFit: Harold Laski was a British political theorist and Labour Party chairman, so Harold is one example of a person with that surname.

clue.text: Gem of a Hawthorne short story about Queen Boudica's first relative

explanation.definitionFit: Nathaniel Hawthorne's story The Great Carbuncle is about a fabled red gemstone sought by adventurers.

clue.text: As one may be after a lean period of fasting, following request

definitions.text: As one may be after a lean

parts.note: to ask is to request

explanation.surface: Someone thin and hungry after a spell of going without food makes a request.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition breaks off at 'lean': the surface makes 'a lean period' one phrase, but 'lean' here means a tilt.
explanation.definitionFit: This Scots word means aslant or askew, which is how something sits after tilting.

clue.text: Effects freely represented in Tremain's stories

parts.note: your kit is your effects or gear

indicators.note: represented means presented again, so the letters of freely are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Possessions are depicted loosely in Rose Tremain's short fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'represented' turns FREELY into EFLYER. Rose Tremain is an English novelist whose story collection The Colonel's Daughter includes a story with this title.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the title of a short story by Rose Tremain, so it appears among her stories.

clue.text: "A mongrel-looking man was —— past. 'Wouldn't he murder you for your watch-chain?'" (D. H. Lawrence, The Primrose Path)

parts.note: a quotation with a word missing: the solver supplies the participle Lawrence used for the man's furtive, sniffing movement

explanation.definitionFit: The word describes moving forward cautiously, like a dog sniffing its way, which suits a mongrel-looking man.

clue.text: Extra hol perhaps for one protecting the environment

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: 'hol' is British slang for a holiday.
explanation.definitionFit: Dr Seuss's Lorax speaks for the trees and tries to stop them being felled.

clue.text: Rivers described by Charlotte Brontë with notes about the Jordan primarily

clue.text: Again saying what Rabb's title character did

a saw is a saying or proverb

explanation.surface: Repeating a remark about what an author's hero was up to.
explanation.walkthrough: Jonathan Rabb's novel The Overseer gives the title character.
